    - *What a sign-in does now.* With the email's cap on failed sign-ins spent (`login.failed`, 30 an hour), no trusted device cookie, and a mailer configured, the sign-in does not refuse. Every attempt gets `202 {"confirm":"email"}`: the same status, body and headers whatever the password, and the same for an unknown email. The attempt sets the nonce cookie on every such answer, so a right and a wrong password differ only in the cookie's random value. Only a right password mails a link, one per matched user. `login.ip` and `login.email` still apply first, so they bound the hashing. Without a mailer the answer is sec1's `429 rate_limited` and its message. Decision 90 changes which passwords a cookie covers: a cookie's own user is tested under its budget, and once the cap is spent the other users get this same answer, while the cookie's user still signs in.
    - *The nonce is per browser, not per attempt.* A request that carries a valid `selfcloud_confirm` cookie keeps that value; a new one is made only for a browser without one. The cookie is set again on every answer, which refreshes its life of `users.device_confirm_ttl`. So every link mailed to a browser binds to the same nonce, any of them works there, and each stays single use. The link's row stores only the hash of the nonce. Test `TestEarlierLinkWorksAfterALaterWrongAttemptInTheSameBrowser`: it passes on the code as built, so it is a guard of the rule, not a red-first test.
    - *The link.* Single use, 15 minutes by default (`users.device_confirm_ttl`, at most 30 minutes), its token stored only as a hash (`device_confirms`, not `verifications`, whose `purpose` CHECK would need a table rebuild, as decision 13 notes). The cookie is `selfcloud_confirm` (`__Host-` over https), HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Path=/. The row keeps the "Keep me signed in" choice of the attempt, so the session it starts keeps that choice.

In the browser that asked, the link signs the user in as a password sign-in does (the same session rules, the old session of this browser replaced, `user.login`), sets the device cookie with the transaction's own issue time (decision 84, F9), and ends the nonce cookie. In another browser: `403 forbidden`, `details.reason` `other_browser`, nothing signed in, and the link is not used up. An unknown, used, expired or voided link: `invalid_request`, as the other links answer. A password change, reset, admin set-password or disable after the mail voids the link: the user's cut-off (`tokens_not_before`) is at or after the link's creation. A pending or disabled user, or a suspended or deleting account, is refused and audited as a sign-in is, and the link is kept.
    - *Mail.* Purpose `device_confirm`, in all seven languages. It says that someone signed in with the password from a new browser, that if it was the person they open this link in that browser, and that if not they do not open it and change their password. It holds no name, password, address or user agent. The row and its `attempted` audit row are written before the mail leaves; the send runs in the background, as a reset's does, and its result row follows.

        - *Catalogues.* The 11 new keys are in all seven languages, none empty and none copied from English (checked by script; `round2/catalogue-check.txt`).

87. **Save As and user info, and the live-run plan, slice l5** (2026-11-05, the owner's choice "Office: Save As + live test"; 86 is sec2, which builds in parallel). Built to the brief's Part A. Part B (a live run against Collabora Online) is prepared, not run. Migration 0047 (`wopi_user_info`; sec2 holds 0045 and ue holds 0046 on this stack).

    - **Sources.** Microsoft Learn's PutRelativeFile and PutUserInfo pages (last updated 2023-03-04), read on 2026-11-05. Collabora's SDK pages (sdk.collaboraonline.com) answer only behind an Anubis proof-of-work challenge that these tools cannot pass, so they were not read. Instead, the same day: Collabora's forum threads on Save As (2021 to 2025; the 2025-07-25 thread quotes `UI_SaveAs`, `Action_SaveAs` with `Filename`, and `Host_PostmessageReady` after the Initialized status); GitHub issue CollaboraOnline/online#14866 (open; Collabora sent no `File_Rename` message in 25.04.9.1); and the ownCloud web PR #13906, which reports a live check against Collabora Online 25.04.7.3.1 (the channel opens when the host answers Host_PostmessageReady; Save As goes UI_SaveAs, then Action_SaveAs, then PutRelativeFile with a suggested target). These are secondary reports, not Collabora's documentation. Microsoft's PutRelativeFile page names `UserCanNotWriteRelative`: a host that sets it true must answer 501 to PutRelativeFile (read on 2026-11-05). The existing code has used that property since l1. `SupportsUserInfo` is not verified: its name is in the MS-WOPI CheckFileInfo response schema (openspecs, read the same day, through a search excerpt), but the property reference page for it was not read.
    - **PutRelativeFile** (`internal/api/office_saveas.go`). A suggested target (an extension, or a full name) never answers 400 or 409: a taken name gets the first free "name (n).ext" (the same rule as `freeName` in transfer.go). An exact target: a free name is created; a taken name without overwrite answers 409 with a free name in X-WOPI-ValidRelativeTarget (UTF-7), so Collabora can retry, and no lock is looked at first (round 2, L5); with overwrite, a token that is not writable answers 501, then a live lock on the target answers 409 with X-WOPI-Lock, and a caller without editor on the target answers 501, as the specification says. Both target headers, or neither, answer 400. Names are UTF-7 (`wopi.DecodeUTF7`).
    - **The directory.** Contributor on the source's directory, which is the upload rule. For a browser-origin token, the check uses the same person with the token's node scope widened to the token's folder list, and its write cap lifted, since a copy may be asked from the read-only view as the specification's example shows (`saveAsPrincipal`). A token minted by a delegated key is never widened (round 3). The copy's token may write only when the caller holds editor on the copy's own node (the new file, or the file it replaced), read with the token's folder list and write cap but not its node scope (round 2, L4).
    - **No-download.** A copy is a download, so a restricted grant (no-download, at viewer or commenter) is refused with 501, and CheckFileInfo answers `UserCanNotWriteRelative` true for it and for any caller without contributor on the directory. Round 2 (rule 4 of the review) made every such refusal a 501, where these two were 404; a node the caller cannot reach at all is still 404. An editor is not bound by no-download (decision 20), and a copy by an editor is allowed.
    - **Writes.** The body goes through `writeBlob` (decision 84): the disk reservation, the account quota before any byte, and `office.max_file_bytes`; a declared `X-WOPI-Size` above the limit is 413 before the body. A failed write removes its blob. A new copy is audited as `node.create`, which reports `file.created` through the existing mapping, with `via: save_as` and `from` the source; an overwrite is `replaceContent` (`node.write`, `file.updated`).
    - **The answer.** `Name` (with the extension); `Url`, the copy's WOPI address with its own token: a new `wps_` session for the same user, carrying the same browser session as the original editor and expiring at the earlier of `office.token_minutes` and the token that asked; `HostEditUrl` and `HostViewUrl`, the Selfcloud editor page for the copy in each mode. The specification makes the host URLs optional; Collabora's use of them is not verified.
    - **PutUserInfo** (`PUT_USER_INFO`, `internal/api/office_userinfo.go`, migration 0047). One string per person, in `wopi_user_info`, which goes with the user (and with the account). A body over 1024 bytes, or one that is not UTF-8, answers 400, a code the operation's page does not list. The page's limit is 1024 ASCII characters; a byte limit is the same for ASCII and stricter otherwise. A browser-origin token with a person may set it, read-only tokens too. A token minted by a delegated key gets 501, since the string is the person's own and the key is not the person (round 2, L6). CheckFileInfo returns `UserInfo` (only when stored) and `SupportsUserInfo: true`, to that person only.
    - **The editor page** (`web/src/pages/OfficeEditPage.tsx`). It answers `App_LoadingStatus` `Initialized` with `Host_PostmessageReady`, sent to the editor's origin only, never "*". On `UI_SaveAs` it opens a dialog with the name without its extension and the extension shown after the field, and sends `Action_SaveAs` with `Values.Filename`. Cancel sends nothing. The four new strings are in seven locales; he, ar, fr, es, ru and pt are machine drafts for a native reader to check.
    - **The fake and the e2e check.** `web/e2e/convertFake.mjs` gains the handshake, a Save As button and a `requestSaveAs()` control (the page polls for it, since the run cannot click inside the frame's origin), PUT_RELATIVE through its own signed call, and PUT_USER_INFO on open. `web/e2e/l4.mjs` runs Save As through the dialog and checks the copy's name and the folder, and checks the UserInfo on the next open.
    - **Tests.** Go: `office_saveas_test.go` (suggested and exact names, free, taken, overwrite, lock, UTF-7, the contributor and no-download refusals, the size, quota and disk-check refusals, the copy's own URL and token, `file.created` and `file.updated`) and `office_userinfo_test.go` (per-user, the boundary, UTF-8, a view token, deletion with the user). `TestWOPIUnimplementedOverridesAnswer501` now checks an override the host does not have. The two guards (`TestNodeKindComparisonsAreReviewed`, `TestEveryNodeWriteIsClassified`) carry the new sites with their reasons. Web: `editor.test.ts` covers the dialog helpers. The tests were written after the code, so there was no red run first; instead, two mutation proofs were made: the lock check disabled (the lock test fails: X-WOPI-Lock is empty) and the UserInfo length rule disabled (the test gets 500, not 400). Each rule was restored and the test rerun green. The full Go suite passes (21 packages), and the full web suite passes (257 files, 2370 tests), `tsc` and the repository's check scripts pass.
    - **The Save As rule (round 2, the review of 335dc28).** One rule decides whether a caller may Save As (`saveAsOffered`). CheckFileInfo, the PUT_RELATIVE handler and the write's own re-check all read it, and a refusal is `UserCanNotWriteRelative` true and a 501. It refuses (1) a token minted by a delegated key: nothing is lifted for it, because the WOPI token keeps none of the delegated token's own cap (its write flag, node and folder list), so any lift could reach past that cap, which was the high finding H1; (2) a no-download file, since a copy is a download; and (3) a caller who may not add files to the file's directory. For a browser-origin token that passes, a new copy is allowed from the read-only view too, which the lift in `saveAsPrincipal` allows. An overwrite needs two things: the source token must be writable (its edit mode), so a view token that asks for one gets 501 and the file is unchanged (H1, M1); and the caller must hold editor on the target itself. The copy's token writes only when the caller's role on the copy's own node is editor or more. The quota pre-check for an overwrite charges the whole new size, as the transaction does (L1). The source is read again inside the write: a source that is gone or in the trash by then is 404, and the copy's directory is the parent read then (L2). The copy's suggested name is also taken from the source as that write reads it, so a rename during the upload is used (round 3). `copyPrincipal` never widens a token minted by a delegated key, so a later change in the order of the write cannot open the high finding again (round 3). A name that a trashed file held is free, since trashing gives the name to the trash (`TrashNode`), so an overwrite of it creates the copy; the round 3 review's expectation of a 409 there was wrong, and the test pins the free name. With all 1000 suggested names taken the answer is 500 with the reason logged, never 409 (L3). PUT_USER_INFO from a delegated token is 501 (L6). The tests written first are in `internal/api/office_saveas_fix_test.go`. Each finding's test was red on 335dc28 and green after. The blob-store check added to the refusal test (L8) passed on both, so it guards the code rather than catching a bug. The round 2 evidence is held outside the repository.
    - **Round 2: the e2e and the artifact.** The editor sections `s4b`, `l4`, `q4` and `pwa` ran against the round 2 binary, built with the web bundle: 115 checks passed and none failed, including Save As through the dialog and the copy's place beside the file. The view-mode refusal is not in the e2e run; it is a step of the manual run. **Not run:** Part B. Part B is a script and a README in `~/.cache/selfcloud-evidence-l5/live/`, with the arm64 artifact there (the round 3 build; its sha256 is recorded in the run folder's README, not here, since a hash in this file would change the commit it names). The script stops at a browser check that is known to fail on that host, so the first real result may be that stop.
    - **Choices the owner may want to confirm.** (a) An overwrite needs editor on the target and an editable (edit-mode) browser-origin token for the source; a contributor who may add files but not replace gets 501, the specification's answer. (b) A browser-origin view may make a new copy when its person has contributor on the folder. A view from a delegated key may not make one. An overwrite from any view answers 501. (c) The copy's token writes only with editor on the copy's own node, so a copy made from a view is read-only, even when its person is an editor of the folder; the view's own cap holds it. (d) The copy's token expires with the earlier of `office.token_minutes` from now and the token that asked. (e) The host pages point at the Selfcloud editor page. (f) UserInfo is capped at 1024 bytes, not characters. (g) `Host_PostmessageReady` is sent on the Initialized status (the 2025 forum reply); the ownCloud report sends it on the frame's load. Only a live run can choose between them.
    - **Not verified.** Collabora's handling of the 501 answer: what the editor shows when a Save As or an overwrite is refused with 501 (the specification's answer for UserCanNotWriteRelative and for an overwrite the token may not make), and whether it offers Save As again from the view. Part B tests this. How Collabora behaves after a copy is saved (whether it reloads the copy, or stays on the original); the exact `UI_SaveAs` values; the `Action_SaveAs` filename form (with the extension, per the forum); whether `PostMessageOrigin` must be set in CheckFileInfo (it is not set here; a forum report says that works); what `SupportsUserInfo` means, against its property reference (not read); and decision 31's F8 list, which is for the live run.

89. **A user's email can be changed through the API, slice ue** (2026-11-05, the owner's choice of the slice, "Email change via API", and his design for it: an account key or an admin only; the new address must be unused; an optional re-verify; sessions kept). Decisions 86 to 88 are other slices written in parallel; this one is 89. The server part and one page of the web interface: the page of the confirmation link, `/email-change`. Migration `0046` (after sec2's 0045; l5 takes 0047, and the loader needs no gaps). The change lives on `PATCH /accounts/{acc}/users/{usr}`, which takes `email`, `verification` and, from an admin session, `admin_password`.
    - *Who may.* An account key may always change a user's address: it can already mint sign-in links for its own users, so this adds no power there. An installation admin, by its **key or its session**, may only with `admin.tenant_access` on, and with tenant access off the change is refused with `403 forbidden` and `details.reason` `tenant_access_off`, as decision 41 refuses every other way in. An admin's session also needs its own password (`admin_password`, checked by `confirmAdminPassword` as way `email_change`). The reason is decision 41: a changed address followed by a password reset by mail is a way into the account, which the admin's ways in are gated against, so the same switch gates it. Both states are tested for the admin key. An account owner session, a member session and a delegated token may not. The owner is refused with `403 forbidden` and `details.reason` `email_caller`. A member or a token does not reach the account at all (`404 not_found`, as every route of an account they do not manage). *Why owners may not:* an owner who could change a member's address could then reset the member's password and read the member's private files. No existing field has a principal refusal in `handleUpdateUser` (an owner may change a role), so this refusal is new; it is the only one in the route.
    - *Checks.* The address goes through `cleanEmail`, as user create does: a bare address, at most 254 bytes, no control characters. A taken address is `409 conflict` (the `UNIQUE (account_id, email_key)` rule, the same message as create). The same address as now (the same lowercased key) is a no-op success: nothing is written, no token is made, and the spelling stored does not change. An installation admin's address is not changed by this route, since no route for an admin's user is changed here (see *Not done*).
    - *`verification`, the same words as user create.* `none` changes the address at once, the default for a key; a session may not use it (`403 forbidden`). `email` mails the confirmation to the **new** address; `link` returns it to the caller, and an admin's key may not take a link to an existing user (decision 41), so `link` is refused for an installation admin's key. A session gets `email` by default.
    - *Pending versus immediate.* With `email` or `link` the old address stays in use and signs in; `pending_email` (new in every user's JSON, `null` when none) shows the new one to whoever sees `email`, and only while its link is live: once the link has expired the request reads as no pending change (round 2, L3). The new address is in `users.pending_email`; its link is a verification of purpose `email_change` in the existing verification store (migration `0046` adds the purpose and rebuilds the table, keeping its rows). `POST /api/v1/auth/email-change/confirm` takes the token: the address applies once, and the link stops working. A newer request replaces the pending one: its token is made by `issueToken`, which voids the earlier tokens of that purpose. An expired link, a replaced one, a used one, and a change that has since been applied are all `400 invalid_request` (`errBadLink`, as verify answers). A disabled user gets `user_disabled`. If another user has the pending address by then, the confirmation is `409 conflict` and the link is not used up. The confirmation lives as long as a verification does (`users.verification_ttl`, 72 hours by default).
    - *What applies a change.* Sessions, device cookies (`tokens_not_before` is not moved) and delegated tokens are kept: it is the same person. The tokens that name the old address are voided: password-reset links, verification links (a pending user's too) and any pending confirmation. The device-confirm links (decision 86) mailed before the change are voided too, in the same transaction, so a link mailed to the old address does not sign in after the change (`VoidDeviceConfirms`; tests `TestAnEmailChangeAtOnceVoidsThePendingDeviceConfirmLink` and `TestAConfirmedLinkChangeVoidsThePendingDeviceConfirmLink`). A reset link issued before the change does not work after it (tested). A change with `none` of a user who never verified makes the user active and verified, as create with `none` does (round 2, L2): the caller vouches for the address, as it may for create. A change with `email` or `link` leaves the status alone, so a pending user stays pending until its confirmation.
    - *The notice.* When a mailer is configured, the old address gets one short mail when the change applies (at once, or on the confirmation), in the user's locale, with no link and no name of the new address (`email_changed` templates, seven languages). The notice is not audited of its own, since the change is (below): a failed send is logged and does not undo the change, and the notice is not the verification mail that decision 74 audits before it leaves. The notice is charged to its own budgets, `mail.notice.account` and `mail.notice` (round 4; round 2 had charged the shared `mail.account` and `mail.target`). When they are spent the change is refused with `429 rate_limited` and a `Retry-After`, and nothing is written, so no change applies without its notice (round 3, N1, below). With no mailer nothing is charged or sent, and the change applies.
    - *Audit.* `user.email_changed` is written when the change applies, with `email` = the new address, as `user.create` already holds the address it creates, and `verification` = `none` or `confirmation`. The old address is not in the entry. A request for a pending change is audited as the mail or link it makes is (`verification.send`, with purpose `email_change`). The uploader fields rule of drop links (section 9, visitors' typed addresses) does not cover a user's own address.
    - *Webhooks: no event.* There is no user-update event (the events are `user.created` and `user.verified`), so none is invented: a change of address queues nothing. A subscriber that needs it reads the user.
    - *Tests.* `internal/api/email_change_test.go`: an installation admin's key refused with `tenant_access_off` and changing the address with it on; a key's change at once (sign-in with the new address and not the old, the session kept, the personal folder kept); an admin session needs its password, with tenant access on; an owner session, a member session and a delegated token are refused and the address is unchanged; a taken address is a conflict, the same address is a no-op, a malformed one and a bad `verification` are refused; a link change is pending until confirmed and confirmed once; a newer request replaces the pending one; an expired link is refused; a reset link from before the change stops working; the notice goes to the old address only when mail is set; the audit entry holds the new address and not the old.
    - *Round 2 (the independent review of 6b90fb3; fixes in their own commits on top).* Each finding has a red run before its fix and a green run after, in `~/.cache/selfcloud-evidence-ue/round2/`. **M1:** the notice is charged to `mail.account` and `mail.target`; `TestNoticesStopWhenTheOldAddressBudgetIsSpent` alternates two addresses for ten changes and finds three notices to each, all ten changes applied (red: five each). Round 3 changes that test (below). **M2:** tests added for the notice on the `none` path (`TestNoneChangeSendsTheOldAddressANoticeWithNoLink`), the email budget (`TestEmailRequestsToOneAddressAreBudgeted`: the fourth request to one address is `429 rate_limited`), a confirmation refused for an address taken since the request (`TestConfirmRefusesAnAddressTakenSinceTheRequest`: `409`, the link not used up), a disabled user (`user_disabled`), a deleted user (`invalid_request`), the confirm audit entry (`TestConfirmIsAuditedAsTheUsersOwnAct`). The owner test asserts `email_caller`; a member and a delegated token are asserted at `404 not_found`, the refusal `managedAccount` gives them, which is the only guard they reach. Each of these tests has a mutation proof, the guard removed and the test red. **L1:** the token check and the second owner-and-admin-session check are removed; one owner check gives `email_caller`. **L2:** a `none` change of a pending user activates it and sets `verified_at`, as create does (`TestNoneVerifiesAPendingUserAsCreateDoes`; the earlier verification link stops working). **L3:** `pending_email` is shown only while its link is live (`TestPendingAddressReadsAsNoneAfterItsLinkExpires`). **L4:** confirm refuses a suspended account (`account_suspended`; that refusal comes from the session and key rules in `auth.go`, and confirm repeats it for the account) and an account being deleted (`conflict`, the refusal `writableAccount` gives a deleting account for writes) (`TestConfirmForASuspendedAccountIsRefused`, `TestConfirmForADeletingAccountIsRefused`).
    - *Choices the owner may want to confirm.* (a) The admin rule above: an account key always, an admin's key or session only with `admin.tenant_access` on. The owner's brief named admin keys; the switch makes them subject to decision 41's gate. (b) Sessions and delegated tokens are kept on a change. (c) Owners and members may not change an address (an owner's refusal is `403`; a member does not reach the route). (d) The old address gets a notice when a mailer is set, with no link and no name of the new address; the notice is **not audited** of its own, since the change is (`user.email_changed`). Its wording is seven drafts, to be read by speakers. (e) The confirmation's life is the verification's, 72 hours (`users.verification_ttl`). (f) The confirmation page is `/email-change` in the web interface, built here: it posts the token to `POST /api/v1/auth/email-change/confirm` on opening and shows done, or that the link is no longer valid (used, expired or replaced), or a failure. Its strings are in the seven catalogues; he and ar are drafts. The default link is in `TestDefaultMailLinksOpenAPage`, which checks it opens a page. (g) The page does not sign the person in: they sign in with the new address. (h) A `none` change of a pending user verifies it, as create with `none` does (round 2, L2). (i) The notice is charged to its own budgets, and a change is refused with `429` when they are spent (round 2, M1; round 3, N1; round 4). (j) **Who can spend each notice budget (round 4; it replaces the N4 wording).** `mail.notice.account` (30 an hour) is keyed by the account, and `mail.notice` (3 an hour) by the account and the old address. Only a change of an address in that account spends them: the account's key, or an installation admin's key or session acting on that account (with `admin.tenant_access` on). Verification mail, invitations, reset mail and forgot-password mail never spend them, and no other tenant or anonymous caller can, so the refusal is self-inflicted. (k) **A failed change gives its charge back, at the time it was charged (round 4; round 5 fixed the time).** The code charges the notice after the change's own writes and before the commit; a refused charge rolls the transaction back. A failure after the charge (a later write in the same request, such as an `external_id` conflict, a commit error, or a panic) refunds the tokens at the reservation's time, because `rate.CancelAt` restores a token only when it is called no later than that time; a refund at a later time restores nothing, which round 4 did in production. Tests: `TestFailedChangesSpendNoNoticeBudget`, and `TestFailedChangesRefundAtTheirReservationTime`, which moves the clock two seconds between the charge and the refund (red on 59cc0ec). The panic case refunds through a deferred call that the commit disarms; no test forces a panic, so that path is covered by the code only.
    - *Round 3 (the reviewer's re-check of a266c61; fixes in their own commit).* Each item has a red run before its fix, in `~/.cache/selfcloud-evidence-ue/round3/`. **Guards (A, B):** `checkEmailChange` refuses a principal with a delegated token (`email_caller`) and calls `requireAdminSession` for a session, so an impersonating session is refused there as defence in depth; the router's `impRefuse` already refuses it. Tests: `TestEmailGuardRefusesATokenPrincipal` and `TestEmailGuardRefusesAnImpersonatingAdminSession` (both call the guard directly), `TestImpersonatingSessionCannotChangeAnEmailEndToEnd` (through HTTP, a regression guard). **N1: a change whose notice cannot be charged is refused.** With a mailer, a `none` change charges its notice budgets for the old address after its own writes, and a confirmation charges them after its writes too (round 4 moved both, and changed the buckets); a spent budget rolls the transaction back. A spent budget answers `429 rate_limited` with `Retry-After` and writes nothing: the address stays, and a pending address stays with its link unused. The notice is sent after the commit and is not charged again. Tests: `TestNoticeBudgetRefusesTheChangeWhenSpent`, `TestConfirmIsRefusedWhenTheOldAddressBudgetIsSpent`, `TestWithoutAMailerNoticesDoNotRefuse`. **N2:** a `none` change that activates a pending user records `activated: true` in its `user.email_changed` entry; a change of an active user records no such key (`TestNoneActivatingAPendingUserIsAudited`). **N3:** the user reads, by ID and the account's list, search `verifications_user` for `pending_until` and never scan `verifications` (`TestUserReadsSearchTheEmailChangeLinks`; the plans are in the evidence folder). No change was needed. **M2:** a confirm-time conflict answers `409` with `reason: email_taken`, which the request-time conflict does not carry, so the two are told apart (`TestConfirmRefusesAnAddressTakenSinceTheRequest`). The deleted-user test is `TestConfirmAfterDeleteFailsByCascade`: `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `verifications` removes the link with the user, so the cascade is what refuses it, not the confirm's own user lookup. **L4:** see the round-2 paragraph.
    - *Round 4 (a cross-tenant denial of service, found by an automated scan of 3adc029).* The notice was charged to `mail.target` (3 an hour per address across the install) and `mail.account`. Other mail spends those too: a create with verification mail from another account spends the target budget of the address it names, so any tenant could spend a victim's address and refuse the victim's own change with 429. Fix: the notice has two buckets that nothing but address changes of the account spend, `mail.notice.account` (30 an hour, keyed by the account) and `mail.notice` (3 an hour, keyed by the account and the old address). They are fixed, like the other mail limits in `server.go`. The notice is still refused with 429 when either is spent, never sent silently. The forgot-password flow spends `mail.forgot.target`, not `mail.target`; the cross-tenant spending came from other accounts' verification mail. Tests, red on 3adc029 (`~/.cache/selfcloud-evidence-ue/round4/`): `TestAnotherAccountsMailDoesNotBlockANoticeOfAChange` and `TestAnotherAccountsMailDoesNotBlockAConfirmation` (another account spends `mail.target` for the victim's address; the victim's change applies, and its notice is sent), and `TestFailedChangesSpendNoNoticeBudget` (three changes fail on an `external_id` conflict; a valid change then applies and its notice is sent). Green on both: `TestNoticeAccountLimitRefusesWhenTheAccountSpendsIt` (the account's 31st change is refused, `mail.notice.account`) and the per-address limit in `TestNoticeBudgetRefusesTheChangeWhenSpent` (`mail.notice`). `TestConfirmIsRefusedWhenTheOldAddressBudgetIsSpent` (round 3) spent the shared `mail.target` through other accounts' mail before round 4; that is no longer what refuses it. It now spends `mail.notice` for the address through the account's own changes, so its refusal is the new bucket's. The plan test `TestUserReadsSearchTheEmailChangeLinks` was run again, unchanged. **Residual, kept on purpose:** a change with `verification: email` still charges `mail.target` for the new address, which other accounts' mail can also spend, so a caller may get 429 for that address. This stays, since `mail.target` protects the person receiving the mail (at most 3 an hour from this installation, whichever account sends it), as user create's verification mail does; a caller that gets the 429 can use `verification: link`, which sends no mail.
    - *Not done.* The field on the user's page of the web interface is not built (the account's own user screen shows the address as before). An installation admin's own address: there is no admin route to change it (`/admins` has create, list and delete only), so the admin branch of the uniqueness rule is not reached by this route, and admins' addresses are left out on purpose. A new browser's confirmation link from slice sec2 is not on this base, so nothing of that kind is voided here; it is for sec2 to add to `voidAddressTokens` when it lands. Follow-ups inherited from create, not fixed by this slice (round 2, L5 and L6): (L5) an address's key is `strings.ToLower` only, so `email_key` needs Unicode normalisation (NFC) and a case fold, with a migration for existing rows: `net/mail` accepts the precomposed and decomposed forms of one address as different keys, and `İ@` folds to `i@`, which collides with the ASCII address. (L6) "unused" is checked only inside the account, as create checks it; an address may repeat across accounts and across the installation admins. Decision 89's "unused" is read here as unused in the account; the design must say whether it means the installation.

90. **A device cookie's budget covers only the user it names, slice sec3** (2026-11-05; 84 is sec1, 86 is sec2, 89 is ue). An automated security review of the pushed sec1 code (main 3c530bf) found a bypass of the per-email cap on failed sign-ins, and the lead confirmed it in the code. Server only; no migration; no new dependency.
    - *What the review found.* A genuine device cookie for any candidate with the email swapped the email's cap (`login.failed`, 30 an hour) for the cookie's own budget (`login.device`, 10 an hour per nonce), and the password was then tested against every candidate with the email. `setDeviceCookie` mints a fresh nonce at every sign-in, so the cookies were not limited. An account owner creates a user with the victim's email in their own account, with `verification: none`, and signs in to get that user's cookie. Through that browser they then guess the password of the victim's user in another account with the same email, outside the cap, and each new sign-in gives ten more guesses an hour. Decision 84, choice (a), had made the cap the only bound across addresses, and this bypassed it.
    - *The rule (as revised in round 2, below).* D is the user the cookie names. `trustedDevice` returns D with the nonce. With a genuine cookie for D and `login.device[nonce]` taken, D's password is tested under the device budget, and the email's cap (`login.failed[email]`) is taken too, whether or not other users have the email. The email's hold covers every candidate tested under it. A failure spends each hold taken. A hold is given back at the reservation's own time (`now`; a later time restores nothing, decision 89 (k)) only when every candidate tested under it matched: the device hold when D matched, and the email's hold when all the candidates did. When the device budget is spent, D is an ordinary candidate under the cap, as without a cookie. So an email held by D alone costs D's device budget and the email's cap, as a failed sign-in does.
    - *When the cap is spent with D holding the device.* If D matches, the sign-in is as D, and the others are not tested. If D does not match, the others are not tested here: with a mailer they go to `confirmByEmail`, which does its own matching, so the hashing stays one check for D and one for each other user; without a mailer they get sec1's refusal. Decision 84's F1 and decision 86 are kept: the cookie's own user still signs in while the cap is spent.
    - *Choice for the owner (corner 3).* With the cap spent, a cookie's user who matches signs in even when another account has the same password. The 409 account choice is lost in that corner, because the other account's password is not tested while the cap is spent. Before the cap is spent, the same sign-in still gets the 409. The owner may want a different answer there. Without a mailer, D's password is checked before the refusal, so a wrong password in that corner costs one check more than a refusal without a cookie does.
    - *Known gap (item 7 of the review; not fixed here).* A cookie for D does not help the same person's retry with `account=B`. `loginScope` narrows the candidates to B, so the cookie names no candidate, `trustedDevice` does not trust it, and the email's cap applies.
    - *No cap on cookie issuance.* The review also suggested capping how many cookies one user can be issued. It is not built. A holder can mint a new cookie only by signing in with that user's password, or by a password reset, which needs the user's mail. A stolen cookie gets its ten guesses an hour and then falls under the email's cap.
    - *Tests.* `internal/api/sec3_device_scope_test.go`, beside the sec1 and sec2 tests. (a) `TestACookieForOneUserDoesNotGuessAnotherUsersPassword`: thirty wrong guesses through the cookie's browser spend the email's cap, so a browser without the cookie is refused (or sent the confirmation), and the cookie's browser's next guess at the other account's password gets no session. (b) `TestWithTheCapSpentTheCookieUserStillSignsIn`: with the cap spent, the cookie's user signs in with the right password. (c) `TestWithTheCapSpentTheCookieBrowserGetsNoSessionForTheOtherUser`: with the cap spent, the other account's right password gets the confirmation with a mailer (202, a mail to that user, no session) and the refusal without one. (d) `TestCorrectSignInsAsOneUserLeaveTheCapWhole` (round 2 changed its setup to one user): thirty correct sign-ins leave the device budget and the email's cap whole, on a clock that moves a millisecond a read. (e) `TestAnEmailHeldByOneUserCountsTheCookieFailuresToo` (round 2 rewrote it): ten wrong guesses through the cookie spend the device budget and the email's cap too. The corner-3 test is `TestCapSpentSamePasswordInTwoAccountsSignsInAsTheCookieUser`.
    - *Red and green.* On abc7a52 (the red tests, commit 7050a0f), (a), (c) and the corner-3 test fail: the cookie's browser gets a session for the other account's password. (b), (d) and (e) pass there as guards. Evidence: `/home/shuki/.cache/selfcloud-evidence-sec3/red-abc7a52.txt`. The fix is commit 8eeea70; the full `internal/api` and `internal/store` suites pass on it, and `gofmt` and `go vet` are clean.
    - *Mutations.* Each one run on the fixed code, and reverted, with the tests it turns red. Evidence files are in the same directory. (1) The email's hold taken for a lone user (`mutation-M1-rule1-email-hold-for-lone-user.txt`): (e) red. (2) The cookie's user not tested while the cap is spent (`mutation-M2-rule3-cookie-user-not-tested-when-capped.txt`): (b) and the corner-3 test red. (3) The other users tested while the cap is spent, instead of going to the cap's answer (`mutation-M3-corner4-tests-all-when-capped.txt`): (c) and the corner-3 test red. (4) The email's hold not given back on a match (`mutation-M4-no-email-hold-refund-on-match.txt`): (d) red. (5) Both holds given back at a later clock read (`mutation-M5-refund-at-a-later-clock-read.txt`): (d) red, the device budget at 0 of 10. (6) The device hold alone, with no email hold, as before the fix (`mutation-M6-old-bug-no-email-hold-with-device.txt`): (a), (c) and the corner-3 test red, and the other account's password signs in. (7) The device hold not given back on a match (`mutation-M8-no-device-hold-refund-on-match.txt`): (d) red. These are the round 1 runs, against the round 1 tests; (d) and (e) were rewritten in round 2.
    - *Round 2 (the independent review of 7050a0f..8b0c89a; each finding, its fix and its test).* The review confirmed that the reported path is closed, and the findings are fixed as follows.
        - *Finding 1 (medium): a match refunded another user's failed test.* Before round 2, a match on any candidate refunded every hold, so a candidate tested in the same request cost nothing. An attacker who owns a user with the victim's email sets that user's password to a guess and signs in with it: the match refunds the email's cap, and the victim's hash has been tested for free. The rule is now the one in the rule bullet above: a hold is given back only when every candidate tested under it matched. Red: `TestAMatchOnOneUserDoesNotRefundTheOtherUsersTest` (thirty sign-ins with the guess spend the cap, so the next wrong guess is refused).
        - *The device hold covers the cookie's user alone.* It is given back only when that user matched, so a match on another user alone does not refund it. Red: `TestAMatchOnAnotherUserAloneDoesNotRefundTheDeviceBudget` (ten sign-ins with the other account's password leave the budget spent).
        - *Choice for the owner (finding 1's cost).* A person with the same email in two accounts and different passwords spends one email token per sign-in, because the other account's password is tested too. Thirty correct sign-ins from the cookie's browser spend the cap; a browser without the cookie is then refused; and the cookie's user still signs in while the cap is spent (F1), with the device budget whole. Test: `TestTwoUsersWithOneEmailSpendOneTokenPerSignIn`. The alternatives are a different answer to that person, or that the other account's password go untested on a sign-in that matched, which the owner has not chosen.
        - *Finding 2 (low): the status oracle.* With a cookie, the email's hold used to be taken only when other users held the email. So a lone user's cookie failures did not count on the cap, while another user's did, and a cookie browser saw 401 for thirty tries on a lone email, and 202 or 429 within thirty tries when another account held it. The status code showed whether another account held the email. Fix: with a trusted device, the email's hold is taken whether or not other users hold the email. The cap-spent corner is the same with or without them: D alone is tested, and a miss goes to `cappedAnswer` for the others, which may be none (`confirmByEmail` then does its dummy check; without a mailer the answer is 429). A lone user's cookie failures spend the cap too, which is fine: the cookie's user still signs in through the corner. Red: `TestAnEmailHeldByOneUserCountsTheCookieFailuresToo` and `TestACookieBrowserSeesTheSameStatusesWhetherOrNotAnotherUserHoldsTheEmail`, which compares the status codes of a lone email and a shared one, with and without a mailer.
        - *The sec1 test that said 401.* `TestDeviceCookieThatFailsItsOwnBudgetStopsBeingTrusted` expected 401 for ten wrong guesses with the cap spent. That answer was the lone-user oracle of finding 2, so those guesses now get the cap's answer (the confirmation with a mailer), as they do when another user holds the email. The test's point, that the right password is refused once the device budget is spent, is unchanged.
        - *Finding 3 (low): audit.* When the cap was spent and the cookie's user failed, that failure was not audited against the cookie's user. Now it is: `auditFailedLogin` writes the cookie user's failed sign-in, as it does for a single candidate, before the others get the cap's answer. With a mailer, `confirmByEmail` writes its one row for the others, so the other account's log has a row too, as a failed sign-in against its own user does; without one, the others get no row, as before. Red: `TestTheCookieUsersFailureWhileCappedIsAudited`, in both variants.
        - *Finding 4 (info): left as written*, in the Known gap and the corner-3 choice above.
        - *Missing tests from the review.* `TestACookieNamingAnotherAccountIsNotTrusted` and `TestACookieIsNotTrustedUnderTheAdminScope`: with a cookie for ann in one account, a sign-in that names another account, or the installation admin scope, does not trust the cookie. The device budget is never taken, and the email's cap applies. Both pass on the round 1 code, as guards: the narrowing was already before the trust check, and the behaviour is unchanged.
        - *Guards that pass on both.* `TestASignInMatchingEveryCandidateRefundsEveryHold`: two users with one password get the 409 thirty times, the device budget stays whole, and the cap is whole afterwards. `TestCorrectSignInsAsOneUserLeaveTheCapWhole`: the lone form of the former test (d), with the moving clock, so a refund at a later time than its reservation would show.
        - *Setup.* Five tests now make the cookie before the other account exists, since a sign-in that tests two users spends a token (`e2deae7`). Only the order changed; the assertions are the same.
